claim: AgRP neurons are activated by energy deficit.
source: AgRP neurons are activated by energy deficit and promote voracious food consumption, suggesting these cells may supply the fundamental hunger drive that motivates feeding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about AgRP neurons.

claim: AgRP neurons promote voracious food consumption.
source: AgRP neurons are activated by energy deficit and promote voracious food consumption, suggesting these cells may supply the fundamental hunger drive that motivates feeding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about AgRP neurons.

claim: AgRP neurons are inhibited within seconds by the sensory detection of food.
source: However recent in vivo recording experiments revealed that AgRP neurons are inhibited within seconds by the sensory detection of food, raising the question of how these cells can promote feeding at all.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from recent in vivo recording experiments.

claim: Brief optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons before food availability promotes intense appetitive and consummatory behaviors that persist for tens of minutes in the absence of continued AgRP neuron activation.
source: Here we resolve this paradox by showing that brief optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons before food availability promotes intense appetitive and consummatory behaviors that persist for tens of minutes in the absence of continued AgRP neuron activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The sustained behavioral responses from AgRP neuron stimulation are mediated by a long-lasting potentiation of the rewarding properties of food.
source: We show that these sustained behavioral responses are mediated by a long-lasting potentiation of the rewarding properties of food and that AgRP neuron activity is positively reinforcing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by conditioned appetite and flavor preference experiments.

claim: AgRP neuron activity is positively reinforcing.
source: We show that these sustained behavioral responses are mediated by a long-lasting potentiation of the rewarding properties of food and that AgRP neuron activity is positively reinforcing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by self-stimulation experiments.

claim: Hunger neurons drive feeding by transmitting a positive valence signal that triggers a stable transition between behavioral states.
source: These findings reveal that hunger neurons drive feeding by transmitting a positive valence signal that triggers a stable transition between behavioral states.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing the experimental findings.

claim: AgRP neurons are regulated by hormones that report on the nutritional state of the body.
source: AgRP neurons are regulated by hormones that report on the nutritional state of the body (Cowley et al., 2001, 2003; Gao and Horvath, 2007; Nakazato et al., 2001; Pinto et al., 2004) and their activity is strongly increased by food deprivation (Hahn et al., 1998; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: AgRP neuron activity is strongly increased by food deprivation.
source: AgRP neurons are regulated by hormones that report on the nutritional state of the body (Cowley et al., 2001, 2003; Gao and Horvath, 2007; Nakazato et al., 2001; Pinto et al., 2004) and their activity is strongly increased by food deprivation (Hahn et al., 1998; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Optogenetic or chemogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons promotes intense food consumption as well as appetitive behaviors that lead to food discovery.
source: Optogenetic or chemogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons promotes intense food consumption as well as appetitive behaviors that lead to food discovery (Aponte et al., 2011; Krashes et al., 2011), whereas inhibition of these neurons leads to aphagia (Gropp et al., 2005; Krashes et al., 2011; Luquet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Inhibition of AgRP neurons leads to aphagia.
source: Optogenetic or chemogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons promotes intense food consumption as well as appetitive behaviors that lead to food discovery (Aponte et al., 2011; Krashes et al., 2011), whereas inhibition of these neurons leads to aphagia (Gropp et al., 2005; Krashes et al., 2011; Luquet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: AgRP neurons are inhibited by the mere sight and smell of food, or by conditioned cues that predict food availability.
source: These experiments unexpectedly revealed that AgRP neurons are inhibited within seconds by the mere sight and smell of food, or by conditioned cues that predict food availability.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from recent in vivo recording experiments.

claim: AgRP neuron inhibition by sensory cues is too fast to be mediated by a hormonal signal.
source: These responses were much too fast to be mediated by a hormonal signal, implying that they arise from changes in neural input.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid timescale of the inhibition.

claim: AgRP neuron inhibition by sensory cues arises from changes in neural input.
source: These responses were much too fast to be mediated by a hormonal signal, implying that they arise from changes in neural input.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid timescale of the inhibition.

claim: AgRP neuron activity is often greatly reduced prior to the onset of feeding.
source: Paradoxically, this rapid inhibition was often complete before a single bite of food could be consumed, such that AgRP neuron activity was greatly reduced prior to the onset of feeding.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from in vivo recording experiments.

claim: Preparatory photostimulation of AgRP neurons triggers intense feeding upon subsequent food presentation.
source: Strikingly, we found that this preparatory photostimulation triggered intense feeding upon subsequent food presentation (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Voracious feeding from AgRP neuron prestimulation approaches the level of food consumption observed following an overnight fast.
source: This voracious feeding approached the level of food consumption observed following an overnight fast (Figure 1E); it did not require learning, as it was observed in the first trial of every mouse (Figure 1—figure supplement 1); and it was absent from control mice that lacked ChR2 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1E comparing prestimulation to fasting.

claim: The feeding response to AgRP neuron prestimulation does not require learning.
source: This voracious feeding approached the level of food consumption observed following an overnight fast (Figure 1E); it did not require learning, as it was observed in the first trial of every mouse (Figure 1—figure supplement 1); and it was absent from control mice that lacked ChR2 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data showing the effect in the first trial of every mouse.

claim: The feeding response to AgRP neuron prestimulation is absent from control mice that lack ChR2 expression.
source: This voracious feeding approached the level of food consumption observed following an overnight fast (Figure 1E); it did not require learning, as it was observed in the first trial of every mouse (Figure 1—figure supplement 1); and it was absent from control mice that lacked ChR2 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prestimulation of AgRP neurons for as little as one minute is sufficient to increase food intake above baseline.
source: Prestimulation of AgRP neurons for as little one minute was sufficient to increase food intake above the baseline level of unstimulated mice (0.34 ± 0.03 vs 0.14 ± 0.03 g, p<0.01), indicating that the response begins to develop rapidly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing 1 minute prestimulation to no stimulation.

claim: Increasing the duration of AgRP neuron prestimulation progressively increases the amount of food consumed, reaching a plateau at approximately 30 min.
source: Increasing the duration of prestimulation progressively increased the amount of food consumed, reaching a plateau at approximately 30 min (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1F showing dose-response relationship.

claim: The relationship between prestimulation duration and subsequent food intake displays first order association kinetics.
source: This relationship between prestimulation duration and subsequent food intake displayed first order association kinetics (Figure 1G; R2 = 0.96), suggesting that AgRP neuron activity transmits a saturable signal that "builds up" in a downstream circuit element.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis in Figure 1G.

claim: AgRP neuron activity transmits a saturable signal that builds up in a downstream circuit element.
source: This relationship between prestimulation duration and subsequent food intake displayed first order association kinetics (Figure 1G; R2 = 0.96), suggesting that AgRP neuron activity transmits a saturable signal that "builds up" in a downstream circuit element.
evidence: This is an inference based on the first order association kinetics observed.

claim: The sustained effects of AgRP neuron activity do not require a specific sequence of light pulses.
source: Consistent with this model, the sustained effects of AgRP neuron activity did not require a specific sequence of light pulses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), although intermittent, high frequency stimulation (20 Hz) was slightly more effective than tonic lower frequency stimulation (10 Hz) at eliciting feeding when the total number of light pulses was held constant.
evidence: This is supported by experiments testing different stimulation patterns.

claim: Intermittent, high frequency stimulation (20 Hz) is slightly more effective than tonic lower frequency stimulation (10 Hz) at eliciting feeding when the total number of light pulses is held constant.
source: Consistent with this model, the sustained effects of AgRP neuron activity did not require a specific sequence of light pulses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), although intermittent, high frequency stimulation (20 Hz) was slightly more effective than tonic lower frequency stimulation (10 Hz) at eliciting feeding when the total number of light pulses was held constant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different stimulation frequencies.

claim: A 30 min delay between the offset of AgRP neuron stimulation and onset of food availability only modestly decreases subsequent food consumption.
source: These sustained effects were long-lasting, as the introduction of a delay of 30 min between the offset of AgRP neuron stimulation and onset of food availability only modestly decreased subsequent food consumption (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1H testing delayed food access.

claim: The long-lasting effects of AgRP neuron prestimulation are manifest primarily as an increase in bout size, rather than bout number.
source: Analysis of the microstructure of feeding revealed that these long-lasting effects were manifest primarily as an increase in bout size, rather than bout number (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of feeding microstructure in Figures 1I and 1J.

claim: AgRP neuron activity transmits a hunger signal that accumulates in a downstream circuit element on a timescale of approximately 30 min.
source: Thus AgRP neuron activity transmits a hunger signal that accumulates in a downstream circuit element on a timescale of approximately 30 min, resulting in a sustained potentiation of feeding that persists even after AgRP neurons have been silenced.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings about prestimulation duration and persistence.

claim: SFONos1 neurons are activated by circulating signals of fluid balance.
source: SFONos1 neurons are activated by circulating signals of fluid balance, and their artificial stimulation is sufficient to drive voracious drinking even in water sated animals (Betley et al., 2015; Oka et al., 2015; Zimmerman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Artificial stimulation of SFONos1 neurons is sufficient to drive voracious drinking even in water sated animals.
source: SFONos1 neurons are activated by circulating signals of fluid balance, and their artificial stimulation is sufficient to drive voracious drinking even in water sated animals (Betley et al., 2015; Oka et al., 2015; Zimmerman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Photostimulation of SFONos1 neurons results in rapid and intense drinking.
source: As previously reported, photostimulation of SFONos1 neurons resulted in rapid and intense drinking (508 ± 68 licks for stimulated animals versus 3 ± 1 licks for controls, p<0.001 Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Prestimulation of SFONos1 neurons for one hour prior to water access has no effect on subsequent water intake.
source: However, unlike AgRP neurons, prestimulation of SFONos1 neurons for one hour prior to water access had no effect on subsequent water intake (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C,D comparing prestimulation to no stimulation.

claim: The persistent mechanism utilized by AgRP neurons to promote feeding does not generalize to SFONos1 neurons.
source: Thus the persistent mechanism utilized by AgRP neurons to promote feeding does not generalize to related ingestive circuits.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison between AgRP and SFONos1 neuron prestimulation effects.

claim: Prestimulation of AgRP neurons causes animals to engage in vigorous lever pressing when levers are subsequently made available.
source: In contrast, prestimulation of AgRP neurons for one hour caused animals to engage in vigorous pressing when the levers were subsequently made available (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Operant responding following AgRP neuron prestimulation is specifically directed toward the food reward.
source: This operant responding was specifically directed toward the food reward, because animals pressed the active lever much more frequently than the inactive lever (223 ± 29 for active lever vs. 28 ± 6 inactive, p<0.001; Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing active and inactive lever presses.

claim: The operant response to AgRP neuron prestimulation is specific to AgRP neuron activation.
source: This response was also specific to AgRP neuron activation, because it was absent from sham stimulated mice that lacked ChR2 expression (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments in Figure 3D.

claim: Prestimulation of AgRP neurons generates long-lasting motivation to work for food that persists in the absence of continued AgRP neuron activity.
source: Thus prestimulation of AgRP neurons generates long-lasting motivation to work for food that persists even in the absence of continued AgRP neuron activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lever pressing experiments.

claim: Both appetitive and consummatory behaviors can be driven by a sustained signal from AgRP neurons.
source: This indicates that both appetitive and consummatory behaviors can be driven by a sustained signal from AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the feeding and lever pressing experiments.

claim: AgRP neurons project to several downstream targets in a primarily one-to-one configuration.
source: AgRP neurons project to several downstream targets in a primarily one-to-one configuration (Betley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH), bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), and lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) are particularly strongly innervated by AgRP neuron axons.
source: Among these, the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH), bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), and lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) are particularly strongly innervated by AgRP neuron axons (Broberger et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neuron terminals in the PVH, BNST, and LHA during feeding can drive voracious food consumption.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neuron terminals in each of these three areas during the act of feeding can drive voracious food consumption (Betley et al., 2013), but it remains unknown whether these same projections support feeding under more physiologic stimulation conditions, in which AgRP neurons are highly active only before food availability.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Prestimulation of AgRP neuron axons in the PVH, BNST, and LHA elicits robust food intake compared to non-stimulated controls.
source: We found that prestimulation of AgRP neuron axons in all of these regions elicited robust food intake compared to non-stimulated controls (PVH: 0.55 ± 0.05 g vs. 0.11 ± 0.02 g, p<0.0001; BNST: 0.38 ± 0.06 g vs. 0.14 ± 0.03 g, p<0.01; LHA: 0.60 ± 0.01 g vs. 0.21 ± 0.05 g, p<0.001 Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sustained response from ARC → PVH projection prestimulation builds up progressively over time.
source: Quantitative analysis of the relationship between prestimulation duration and food intake for ARC → PVH projections revealed that this sustained response built up progressively over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with kinetics similar to those observed for prestimulation of the soma (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sustained effects of AgRP projection prestimulation are unaffected by a 10 min delay between laser offset and the onset of food availability.
source: These sustained effects were unaffected by the introduction of a 10 min delay between laser offset and the onset of food availability, indicating that they persist in the absence of ongoing feeding behavior (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: AgRP neuron projections to the PVH, BNST, and LHA all support vigorous and specific lever pressing following prestimulation.
source: All three projections supported vigorous and specific lever pressing (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) to an extent that was comparable to the effect of stimulating all AgRP neurons in the ARC (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At least three different projections of AgRP neurons are individually sufficient to elicit the sustained feeding behavior that arises from AgRP neuron activity.
source: Thus, at least three different projections of AgRP neurons are individually sufficient to elicit the sustained feeding behavior that arises from AgRP neuron activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the projection-specific prestimulation experiments.

claim: Food deprivation enhances the positively rewarding properties of food.
source: One important mechanism by which food deprivation motivates feeding is by enhancing the positively rewarding properties of food, such as its palatability (Berridge, 2004, 2009; Cabanac, 1971; Fulton, 2010; Lockie and Andrews, 2013; Rolls et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A single trial of AgRP neuron prestimulation can generate conditioned appetite for subsequently presented food.
source: This indicates that a single trial of AgRP neuron prestimulation can generate conditioned appetite for subsequently presented food.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the conditioned appetite experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Conditioned appetite from AgRP neuron prestimulation is specific to the test conditions associated with AgRP neuron prestimulation.
source: This conditioned appetite was specific to the test conditions associated with AgRP neuron prestimulation, because it was not prevented by ad libitum access to chow in the home cage (Figure 5A) and was completely absent from sham stimulated control mice (Figure 5B, gray).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Providing mice with overnight access to test pellets abolishes the conditioned appetite in the next trial.
source: This was indeed the case: providing the mice with overnight access to the test pellets abolished the conditioned appetite in the next trial (Figure 5B,C red).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5B,C showing extinction.

claim: AgRP neuron activity can condition appetite for specific foods that are consumed after AgRP neurons have shut off.
source: Thus AgRP neuron activity can condition appetite for specific foods that are consumed after AgRP neurons have shut off, such that these foods are later consumed in the absence of homeostatic need.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the conditioned appetite experiments.

claim: AgRP neuron prestimulation can attribute incentive value to the sensory properties of subsequently consumed food.
source: This suggests that AgRP neuron prestimulation can attribute incentive value to the sensory properties of subsequently consumed food.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conditioned appetite experiments.

claim: Conditioning with AgRP neuron prestimulation robustly reverses mice's flavor preference.
source: We found that this conditioning protocol robustly reversed the mice's flavor preference, such that the less preferred flavor became more preferred (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5E.

claim: Animals learn to prefer flavors that are preceded by AgRP neuron activation.
source: Thus, animals learn to prefer flavors that are preceded by AgRP neuron activation, consistent with the idea that AgRP neuron activity induces a long-lasting potentiation of the rewarding sensory properties of food.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the flavor preference experiments.

claim: Mice fail to perform operant responses in order to shut off AgRP neuron activity.
source: Of note, a previous study reported that mice failed to perform operant responses in order to shut off AgRP neuron activity, indicating that these neurons do not motivate behavior by negative reinforcement (Betley et al., 2015), which we confirmed independently (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and confirmed by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: AgRP neurons do not motivate behavior by negative reinforcement.
source: Of note, a previous study reported that mice failed to perform operant responses in order to shut off AgRP neuron activity, indicating that these neurons do not motivate behavior by negative reinforcement (Betley et al., 2015), which we confirmed independently (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and confirmed by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice engage in lever pressing in order to optically stimulate their AgRP neurons.
source: Strikingly, we found that mice engaged in lever pressing in order to optically stimulate their AgRP neurons (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6B.

claim: Lever pressing for AgRP neuron self-stimulation is highly biased toward the active versus inactive lever.
source: This lever pressing was specifically directed toward AgRP neuron self-stimulation, because it (1) was highly biased toward the active versus inactive lever (Figure 6B,H), (2) was greatly reduced in control mice that lacked ChR2 expression (Figure 6H), and (3) underwent rapid extinction when the active lever was uncoupled from the laser (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6B,H.

claim: Lever pressing for AgRP neuron self-stimulation is greatly reduced in control mice that lack ChR2 expression.
source: This lever pressing was specifically directed toward AgRP neuron self-stimulation, because it (1) was highly biased toward the active versus inactive lever (Figure 6B,H), (2) was greatly reduced in control mice that lacked ChR2 expression (Figure 6H), and (3) underwent rapid extinction when the active lever was uncoupled from the laser (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments in Figure 6H.

claim: Lever pressing for AgRP neuron self-stimulation undergoes rapid extinction when the active lever is uncoupled from the laser.
source: This lever pressing was specifically directed toward AgRP neuron self-stimulation, because it (1) was highly biased toward the active versus inactive lever (Figure 6B,H), (2) was greatly reduced in control mice that lacked ChR2 expression (Figure 6H), and (3) underwent rapid extinction when the active lever was uncoupled from the laser (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6D.

claim: Mice engage in repeated cycles of lever pressing followed by food consumption during AgRP neuron self-stimulation.
source: First, we observed reliable temporal coordination between lever pressing and food intake in mice allowed to self-stimulate: mice engaged in repeated cycles of lever pressing followed by food consumption (Figure 6E,F), whereas food consumption was greatly reduced when the lever was uncoupled from the laser (1.5 ± 0.2 g for active laser vs. 0.39 ± 0.07 g for inactive laser, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Food consumption is greatly reduced when the lever is uncoupled from the laser during self-stimulation experiments.
source: First, we observed reliable temporal coordination between lever pressing and food intake in mice allowed to self-stimulate: mice engaged in repeated cycles of lever pressing followed by food consumption (Figure 6E,F), whereas food consumption was greatly reduced when the lever was uncoupled from the laser (1.5 ± 0.2 g for active laser vs. 0.39 ± 0.07 g for inactive laser, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing active and inactive laser conditions.

claim: Strong induction of Fos is observed in AgRP neurons from mice allowed to lever press for self-stimulation.
source: Second, we observed strong induction of the activity marker Fos in AgRP neurons from mice allowed to lever press for self-stimulation, whereas no Fos was observed in otherwise identical trials in which the laser was inactivated (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice will actively lever press in order to stimulate their AgRP neurons, indicating that the activity of these cells is positively reinforcing.
source: Thus mice will actively lever press in order to stimulate their AgRP neurons, indicating that the activity of these cells is positively reinforcing under these conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the self-stimulation experiments.

claim: Mice trained to lever press in the presence of food will self-stimulate AgRP neurons in a trial that lacks food.
source: First, we tested whether mice trained to lever press in the presence of food would self-stimulate in a trial that lacked food. We found that they did, as self-stimulation remained robust even when food was absent during the trial (Figure 6C,H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6C,H.

claim: The presence of food is not acutely required for the positively reinforcing effects of AgRP neuron activity.
source: This indicates that the presence of food is not acutely required for the positively reinforcing effects of AgRP neuron activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the self-stimulation experiments without food.

claim: Mice trained to lever press for AgRP neuron stimulation without food engage in minimal lever pressing indistinguishable from control mice.
source: Under these conditions, we found that mice engaged in minimal lever pressing that was indistinguishable from control mice that lacked ChR2 expression (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6G,H.

claim: AgRP neuron stimulation is not intrinsically rewarding.
source: This indicates that AgRP neuron stimulation is not intrinsically rewarding (hypothesis 1), but that prior experience self-stimulating AgRP neurons in the presence of food is sufficient for lever pressing to become positively reinforcing in food's absence (hypothesis 2b).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of self-stimulation with and without food training.

claim: Prior experience self-stimulating AgRP neurons in the presence of food is sufficient for lever pressing to become positively reinforcing in food's absence.
source: This indicates that AgRP neuron stimulation is not intrinsically rewarding (hypothesis 1), but that prior experience self-stimulating AgRP neurons in the presence of food is sufficient for lever pressing to become positively reinforcing in food's absence (hypothesis 2b).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of self-stimulation with and without food training.

claim: The sustained positive valence signal from AgRP neurons is sufficient to condition both Pavlovian and instrumental learning.
source: This sustained positive valence signal is sufficient to condition both Pavlovian and instrumental learning, and likely accounts for much of the behavioral response that is elicited by AgRP neuron activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the conditioned appetite and self-stimulation experiments.

claim: Stimulation of AgRP neurons for as little as one minute is sufficient to increase subsequent food intake over baseline.
source: We have shown that stimulation of AgRP neurons for as little as one minute is sufficient to increase subsequent food intake over baseline (Figure 1F); that this hunger signal builds up progressively over the course of 30–60 min, until prestimulated animals eat nearly as much food as mice fasted overnight (Figure 1E); and that this dramatic response is robust to insertion of a delay of tens of minutes between the offset of AgRP neuron stimulation and the onset of feeding (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Figure 1.

claim: The hunger signal from AgRP neurons builds up progressively over the course of 30–60 min.
source: We have shown that stimulation of AgRP neurons for as little as one minute is sufficient to increase subsequent food intake over baseline (Figure 1F); that this hunger signal builds up progressively over the course of 30–60 min, until prestimulated animals eat nearly as much food as mice fasted overnight (Figure 1E); and that this dramatic response is robust to insertion of a delay of tens of minutes between the offset of AgRP neuron stimulation and the onset of feeding (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Figure 1.

claim: The dramatic feeding response to AgRP neuron prestimulation is robust to insertion of a delay of tens of minutes between the offset of AgRP neuron stimulation and the onset of feeding.
source: We have shown that stimulation of AgRP neurons for as little as one minute is sufficient to increase subsequent food intake over baseline (Figure 1F); that this hunger signal builds up progressively over the course of 30–60 min, until prestimulated animals eat nearly as much food as mice fasted overnight (Figure 1E); and that this dramatic response is robust to insertion of a delay of tens of minutes between the offset of AgRP neuron stimulation and the onset of feeding (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Figure 1.

claim: The entire hunger drive that motivates food seeking and consumption is transferred to a downstream circuit node during AgRP neuron firing.
source: This suggests that the entire "hunger drive" that motivates food seeking and consumption is transferred to a downstream circuit node during AgRP neuron firing, such that this drive becomes independent of continued AgRP neuron activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sustained effects on both appetitive and consummatory behaviors.

claim: The sustained potentiation of feeding results from a stable change in the internal state of the mouse.
source: The fact that these effects are robust to the introduction of a 30 min delay implies that they must result from a stable change in the internal state of the mouse, rather than some feedback process that requires interaction with food.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of effects with delayed food access.

claim: The persistent orexigenic effects of AgRP neuron activity do not depend on a single circuit node.
source: Thus the persistent orexigenic effects of AgRP neuron activity do not depend on a single circuit node.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the finding that multiple projections can drive sustained feeding.

claim: AgRP neurons express two neuropeptides that regulate feeding: NPY and AgRP.
source: One mechanism for the generation of persistent neural activity is the release of neuromodulators (Major and Tank, 2004), and AgRP neurons express two neuropeptides regulate feeding, NPY and AgRP (Clark et al., 1985; Fan et al., 1997; Hahn et al., 1998; Ollmann et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NPY has been shown to induce long-lasting changes in membrane excitability and neurotransmitter release in certain contexts.
source: In slice, NPY has been shown to induce long-lasting changes in membrane excitability and neurotransmitter release in certain contexts (Dubois et al., 2012; Fu et al., 2004; Roseberry et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Injections of NPY into the brain can drive voracious feeding with kinetics and duration that vary depending on the protocol.
source: In addition, injections of NPY into the brain can drive voracious feeding with kinetics and duration that vary depending on the protocol (Clark et al., 1985; Morley et al., 1987a; 1987b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The AgRP neuropeptide can potentiate food intake for as long as two weeks in certain contexts.
source: Unlike NPY, the AgRP neuropeptide can potentiate food intake for as long as two weeks in certain contexts (Hagan et al., 2000; Krashes et al., 2013; Nakajima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The release of the AgRP neuropeptide requires at least two hours to affect feeding.
source: By contrast the release of the AgRP neuropeptide requires at least two hours to affect feeding (Krashes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The AgRP neuropeptide acts too slowly to explain the immediate feeding response to AgRP neuron prestimulation.
source: Thus the AgRP neuropeptide appears to act too slowly to explain our findings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timescale of AgRP neuropeptide action versus the immediate feeding response.

claim: AgRP neuron projections to the BNST function by targeting BNST neurons that do not express the melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R).
source: However AgRP neuron projections to the BNST have been shown to function by targeting BNST neurons that do not express the melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R), which is the target of AgRP (Garfield et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The AgRP neuropeptide cannot be the molecule that drives feeding in ARC → BNST stimulation experiments.
source: This implies that the AgRP neuropeptide cannot be the molecule that drives feeding in our ARC → BNST stimulation experiments, and therefore that other neurotransmitters released by these cells (GABA or NPY) must underlie their sustained effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that BNST targets do not express MC4R.

claim: Other neurotransmitters released by AgRP neurons (GABA or NPY) must underlie the sustained effects of ARC → BNST stimulation.
source: This implies that the AgRP neuropeptide cannot be the molecule that drives feeding in our ARC → BNST stimulation experiments, and therefore that other neurotransmitters released by these cells (GABA or NPY) must underlie their sustained effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that BNST targets do not express MC4R.

claim: Prior AgRP neuron stimulation robustly conditions flavor and food preference.
source: We found that prior AgRP neuron stimulation robustly conditioned flavor and food preference (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: AgRP neuron prestimulation is sufficient to motivate mice following a single trial to overeat a test food that had been paired with AgRP neuron prestimulation.
source: This effect was sufficient to motivate mice following a single trial to overeat a test food that had been paired with AgRP neuron prestimulation (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5B,C.

claim: AgRP neurons motivate feeding by potentiating the incentive salience or perceived rewarding properties of food encountered during a state of energy deficit.
source: The finding that this food-specific craving can be trained by AgRP neuron prestimulation argues that these neurons motivate feeding by potentiating the incentive salience or perceived rewarding properties of food encountered during a state of energy deficit (Seeley and Berridge, 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the conditioned appetite experiments.

claim: Food deprivation can magnify food reward.
source: Of note, the idea that food deprivation can magnify food reward has long been recognized as a critical mechanism that drives feeding (Berridge, 2004; Cabanac, 1971), but the underlying neural mechanisms have been unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: AgRP neurons are the origin of the effect by which food deprivation magnifies food reward.
source: We propose that AgRP neurons are the origin of this effect.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: AgRP neuron activity attains positive valence specifically in the presence of food.
source: This argues that AgRP neuron activity is not necessarily intrinsically rewarding, but that it attains positive valence specifically in the presence of food.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the self-stimulation experiments with and without food.

claim: AgRP neurons enhance food's intrinsically rewarding properties.
source: This observation is again most readily explained by a model in which AgRP neurons enhance food's intrinsically rewarding properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the self-stimulation and conditioning experiments.

claim: Animals do not self-administer aversive stimuli.
source: By contrast, these findings do not support a model in which AgRP neurons motivate food consumption primarily through a negative valence signal (Betley et al., 2015), since animals do not self-administer aversive stimuli.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about animal behavior.

claim: AgRP neurons transmit a positive valence signal that can robustly condition appetite and motivate instrumental responding.
source: This has revealed that AgRP neurons transmit a previously unsuspected positive valence signal that can robustly condition appetite (Figure 5) and motivate instrumental responding (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Both positive and negative valence mechanisms contribute to the control of feeding behavior.
source: Indeed, there is evidence that both positive and negative valence mechanisms contribute to the control of feeding behavior (Berridge, 2004; Bindra, 1976; Fulton, 2010; Hull, 1943; Lockie and Andrews, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.
